REASONS
8. Issue No.1 :- It is the case of the plaintiff that the suit schedule properties were acquired by their
father Muddappa under the partition deed dated 10.04.1972, which was affected between four sons
of Nanjundappa. A careful scrutiny of the materials on record reveal that the neither the claim of the
plaintiff with the regard to the acquisition of the suit properties by Muddappa under the partition
dated 10.4.1972 nor the O.S. No.5782/2016 claim of the plaintiff in the suit properties are disputed
by the defendants. A conjoint reading of written statement averments at paragraph no. 4, 5 and 7
disclose that the defendants have categorically admitted the entitlement of the plaintiff to the extent
of 1/3rd share in the suit properties but they have fundamentally defended the claim on the ground
of non availability of the suit properties for partition. No doubt Section 53 of the Bharatiya Sakhsya
Adhiniyam, 2023 ( herein after referred as BSA) the erstwhile Section 58 Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
provides that no fact needs to be proved in any proceeding which the parties thereto or their agents
agree to admit at the hearing, or which, before the hearing, they agree to admit by any writing under
their hands, or which by any rule of pleading in force at the time they are deemed to have admitted
by their pleadings but the proviso of Section 53 of the BSA provides that the Court may, in its
discretion, require the facts admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admissions. In the above
case the plaintiff has not pleaded the details of the O.S. No.5782/2016 acquisition of the suit
properties from her great grand father in the plaint or produced any other documents evidencing
the flow of title under Section 6 of the Amended Hindu Succession Act, 1956 . Meanwhile the issue
no.1 framed by the court indicates that this court has not chosen to hold that the suit properties are
the ancestral properties owing to the judicial admission of the defendants in the written statement
but instead the court has directed the parties to lead evidence and consequentially the evidence led
Sulochana M vs Mahesh M on 28 January, 2026

in this context has to be examined notwithstanding the defendants' admission in the written
statement on the mode of acquisition of the suit properties by Mudappa.
9. In the instant case the plaintiff is claiming the right through her deceased father namely Mudappa
without indicating that the suit properties were acquired through her paternal ancestors upto three
degrees above her. The Hon'ble Apex Court of India between Arshnoor Singh V/s Harpal Kaur and
Others, reported in (2020) 14 SCC 436 at para 7.3 held that under Mitakshara law, whenever a male
ancestor inherits any O.S. No.5782/2016 property from any of his paternal ancestors upto three
degrees above him, then his male legal heirs upto three degrees below him, would get an equal right
as coparceners in that property. The Hon'ble Apex Court of India in Vineeta Sharma V/s Rakesh
Sharma & Others (Supra) at Page 34 Para 24 has held that a coparcenary property is the one which
is inherited by a Hindu from his father, grandfather, or great grandfather. Property inherited from
others is held in his rights and cannot be treated as forming part of the coparcenary. The property in
coparcenary is held as joint owners. The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in RFA NO. 1925/2006 in
the case of Basavaraj Meti and another v. Prema bai Jamadar and others, while answering the point
on whether the property inherited under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, acquires the
characteristic of a co- paracenery property subsequent to the division of properties between two
brothers vis-à-vis sons of the parties to the partition, has held that coparcenary is a creature of the
statute and it cannot be created by way of an agreement. That being the O.S. No.5782/2016 position
the conduct of the parties will not change the characteristics of the property. It is appropriate to
extract para 18 of the above judgment :
"18. It is required to be noticed that the Act is watershed movement when it comes to
succession among Hindus. The Act deals with both testamentary as well as
non-testamentary succession both in respect of coparcenary properties as well as self
acquired properties. In addition to that, Section 4 of the Act has a far reaching
consequence as the said provision has an overriding effect in respect of all matters for
which the provision is made in the Act. As far as succession is concerned,there is no
dispute that Sections 6, 8, 15 and 1 9 of the Act are the provisions governing the
succession to the properties of a Hindu. From reading of these provisions, it is
abundantly clear that the parliament in its wisdom wanted to do away with the
concept of the birth right in respect of properties governed under Section 8 of the Act.
This being the position, this Court is of the view that merely because Kanaksingh and
Raghunathsingh effected a partition between themselves in respect of the properties
which they inherited under Section 8 of the Act, the character of the property will not
change. The nature of the property has to be determined with reference to the nature
of acquisition after the O.S. No.5782/2016 demise of the holder of the property. If the
holder of the property dies leaving behind the self acquired property, then the
property would devolve under Section 8 of the Act. If the holder dies leaving behind
his share in the coparcenary property, then Section 6 of the Act would come into
picture provided other circumstances enumerated in Section 6 of the Act are met
with.".

10. From the above judgments it is pellucid that in order to claim a share in the coparcenary
property the plaintiff has to necessarily prove that the property sought to be partitioned is a
Mitakshara coparcenary property inherited from his paternal ancestors upto three degrees above
him. In the case on hand it is not the case of the plaintiff that suit properties were the coparcenary
property of her great grandfather and the father of the plaintiff had acquired rights over the suit
properties under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. There is nothing on record to prove
that the great grand father of the plaintiff had acquired the suit properties from his paternal
ancestors upto three degrees above him. .When the plaintiff is O.S. No.5782/2016 claiming
coparcenary rights in the suit properties it is incumbent upon the plaintiff to plead and prove that
her father leaving behind his share in the coparcenary property.
11. The plaint averments are bereft of the material particulars of the same. Mere plea of partition
between the children of Nanjundappa on 10.4.1972 without providing any material particulars of the
mode of acquisition of the properties is not sufficient to hold that the suit properties are the
ancestral and coparcenary properties. The execution of the partition deed between the family
members in respect of properties left behind by the holder of the properties would not change the
character of the properties from self acquired properties to that of coparcenary properties. As held
in the above judgments coparcenary is a creature of the statute and it cannot be created by way of an
agreement and thus no presumption of coparcenary property can be drawn. It is not the case of the
plaintiff that properties devolved upon the children of Nanjundappa were inherited from their
paternal ancestors up O.S. No.5782/2016 to three degrees above them and they had affected
partition in respect of such properties . Even the genealogical tree produced by the plaintiff at Ex.P1
does not go beyond Nanjundappa, who is the paternal grand father of the plaintiff. There are no
particulars specifying the names of the paternal ancestors of the plaintiff in the family tree upto
three degrees above the plaintiff in the plaint. Ex.P3 and P4 merely disclose that the properties
allotted to Mudappa in respect of Sy. NO. 47/1 , Sy. NO. 256/3 and Sy. NO. 261/2 on the basis of the
partition on 10.4.1972 were mutated in the revenue records. None of the documents produced by the
plaintiff in the form of RTC extracts and encumbrance certificates would be of any assistance to
prove the the suit properties are the ancestral properties . A perusal of the RTC extracts produced at
Ex.P5 to 17 , Ex.P23 to 26, Ex.P51, Ex.P52, Ex.P55 , Ex.P 57, Ex.P58, Ex.P61 standing in the name of
Malleshaih with reference to Sy. NO. 167/3 , 167/2 , Sy. NO. 166/3 , 100/1B , Sy. NO. 256/3, 167/P3
; the RTC extracts at Ex.P18 , Ex.P20 & 22 , Ex.P56, Ex.P 62 which are O.S. No.5782/2016 standing
in the name of Mudappa with reference to Sy. 47/1, Sy. No. 256/3 & P56; the RTC extracts standing
in the name of Nanjundappa at Ex.P19 & 21with reference to Sy. No. 47/1 ; the RTC extract at
Ex.P53 & 59 in respect of Sy. No. 256/3 in the name of Puttamariayyappa , Mudappa and
Gouramma , the RTC extract at Ex.P54, 60 in respect of Sy. No. 261/ 2 in the name of Puttaiah and
Mudappa; Similarly the RTC extracts at Ex.P27 and 28 which disclose the name of Malleshaiah,
Puttaiah, Puttamarriappa and Mudappa in respect of Sy. No. 256/3 or the RTC extracts at Ex.P29
and 30 standing in the name of Puttaiah and Mudappa in respect of Sy. No. 261/2, would not come
to the aid and assistance of the plaintiff to substantiate that the suit properties are the ancestral and
coparcenary properties. In State of Himachal Pradesh Vs. Keshar Ram and others, reported in 1996
(11) SCC 257 the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that "the entries in the revenue papers, by no stretch
of imagination can from the basis for declaration of title in favour of the plaintiff". The Hon'ble O.S.
No.5782/2016 Supreme Court further held that even if the entries in record of rights carry
Sulochana M vs Mahesh M on 28 January, 2026

evidentiary value, that itself would not confer any title on the plaintiff on the suit land in question.
Thus even if some of the properties are found to be standing in the name of Mudappa in the RTC
extracts the same would not confer any coparcenary right on the plaintiff.
12. The reliance on Ex.P63, which is the certified copy of the Panchayat Parikath dtd. 10.4.1972 in
terms of which the father of the plaintiff was allotted the suit properties is not at all of any assistance
to the plaintiff as the recitals of the panchayat parikath clearly demonstrate that the said document
is not a record of past transaction as it could be deduced that the document in-fact created right title
and interest of the parties in the party of dispute for the first time. Therefore when the said
document is creating rights in favor of the parties to the document it is compulsory registrable
under Section 17 of the Registration Act and in the absence of registration the same cannot be
admitted in evidence. At this stage it is relevant to O.S. No.5782/2016 refer to Para 14 of the
Judgment of the Venkataswamy and other V/s Annemma ILR 2015 KAR 4715 wherein it is held that
if the parties in unequivocal terms have agreed to partition by metes and bonds and accordingly the
property has fallen to their respective shares, and if from the date of the partition they have become
the owner of the exclusive properties mentioned in the schedule then it is only from that day except
the blood relationship all other relationship should extinguished. Further if an oral partition has
been affected between the parties and subsequently the same has been reduced into writing as a
Memorandum of Partition in the joint family as the evidence of partition then no registration is
required. In the above case the recitals of the panchayat parikath reveal that the parties had
mutually agreed to enjoy their respective shares and so also remit taxes in respect of their shares
from the date of partition and consequently it can be deduced that there was partition by metes and
bounds under the said document itself which necessitated registration of the document. Upon
failure of O.S. No.5782/2016 registration of the document the consequence enumerated under
Section 49(c) of the Registration Act would follow and in the result the said document cannot be
received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property.
13. Additionally it is also found that the said document cannot also be used for collateral purpose as
the plaintiff has filed the suit seeking partition in respect of the properties which are the subject
matter of the panchayat parikath . In Kaladevi vs V.R.Somasundaram & Ors , 1 AIR 2010 SUPREME
COURT 1654, the Apex Court, referred to K.B Saha and sons V/s Development Consultant Limited,
2008) 8 SCC 564, wherein the Apex Court had culled out the following principles:-
1. A document required to be registered, if unregistered is not admissible into
evidence under Section 49 of the Registration Act.
2. Such unregistered document can however be used as an evidence of collateral
purpose as provided in the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act.
O.S. No.5782/2016
3. A collateral transaction must be independent of, or divisible from, the transaction to effect which
the law required registration.
Sulochana M vs Mahesh M on 28 January, 2026

4. A collateral transaction must be a transaction not itself required to be effected by a registered
document, that is, a transaction creating, etc. any right, title or interest in immovable property of the
value of one hundred rupees and upwards.
5. If a document is inadmissible in evidence for want of registration, none of its terms can be
admitted in evidence and that to use a document for the purpose of proving an important clause
would not be using it as a collateral purpose."
14. Therefore from the above principles it is abundantly evident that the panchayat parikhat at
Ex.P63 cannot be used as evidence as it is not independent of, or divisible from, the transaction to
effect which the law required registration. Notwithstanding the non registration of the partition
deed at Ex.P63, and assuming for a moment that the said document is admissible in evidence then

17. At this stage it is pertinent to refer to Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, which provides
that any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, and who has reasonable
apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding may cause him serious injury, may sue to
have it adjudged void or voidable; and the court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to
be delivered up and canceled. Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act provides that all agreements are
contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful
consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void. Section 19
of the Indian Contract Act provides that when consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud
or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent
was so caused. It is not the O.S. No.5782/2016 case of the plaintiff that the defendants prevented the
Sub Registrar from examining the plaintiff about the execution of the relinquishment deed at
Ex.P65 at the time of registration. No allegations of collusion are made against the Sub Registrar by
the plaintiff. Section 34(3) of the Registration Act, 1908, provides that the registering officer shall
enquire whether or not such document was executed by the persons by whom it purports to have
been executed and satisfy himself as to the identity of the persons appearing before him and alleging
that they have executed the document. While Section 34(1) of the said Act provides that no
document shall be registered under this Act,unless the persons executing such document, or their
representatives, assigns or agents authorized as aforesaid, appear before the registering officer
within the time allowed for presentation . In this regard it is also relevant to refer to Section 35 of
the said Act wherein the procedure on admission and denial of execution has been provided. In this
context, Section 35 (3) (a) of the Act mandates that if any person by whom the O.S. No.5782/2016
document purports to be executed denies its execution, the registering officer shall refuse to register
the document as to the person so denying. In the above case there are absolutely no averments in
the plaint as to how the enquiry before the Sub registrar was conducted and if at all any enquiry was
conducted why the plaintiff failed to report the factum of fraudulent misrepresentation to the sub
registrar. It is not the case of the plaintiff that no such enquiry was conducted and the sub- registrar
had acted in collusion with the defendants in failing to comply with mandatory provisions of the
Registration Act, 1908. It is also not the case of the plaintiff that the sub registrar proceeded to
register the relinquishment deed in spite of her denial of the execution. When the plaintiff was not
allowed the read the contents of the draft of the relinquishment deed she could not have admitted
the contents of the same during the enquiry before the Sub registrar. When the plaintiff has not
challenged the process of registration and admitted the document before the sub registrar at the
time of execution it is O.S. No.5782/2016 deemed that all the statutory requirements were complied

facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument or decree canceled or set aside or the contract
rescinded first become known to him. But the explanation - 3 of T.P.Act provides that a registration
of a document is deemed knowledge of the factum of registration. In Janardhanam Prasad v.
Ramdas (2007) 15 SCC 174, the Supreme Court relying on Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act,
1882 has held that a person is said to have notice' of a fact when he actually knows that fact, or when
but for wilful absentation from an enquiry or search which he ought to have made , or gross
negligence, he would have known it.The explanation of Section 3 further provides that, any person
acquiring any immovable property or any part of, or share or interest in, such property shall be
deemed to have notice of the title if any person who is for time being in actual possession thereof. It
is held that the principle of constructive notice is applicable in respect of registered instrument. The
